owner: W1-FACTIONS — the three carried faction questlines
why: Every `opens_by.topic` and `opens_by.prerequisite_topics` value on the Wet Ledger, Imperial
Assize and Xul-Aneekh questlines has its body here. The project's most expensive defect was
that 74 of 76 `opens_by.topic` values could not be satisfied by any edge the machine can
fire, and it was invisible because every quest tool seeded the gate with the quest's own
string. So: a topic with no info is a keyword nobody in the province can say out loud, and
a keyword nobody can say is a quest nobody can be offered.
Each topic carries at least two infos from different actors, because RI-DLG01 requires a
keyword to be answerable by more than one kind of person, and because a line spoken only by
the quest giver is a briefing rather than a conversation. `to` edges are the AddTopic graph
topic-supply.js reads: asking about one thing teaches you the words for the next.
Disposition gates (`d`) are real. The Ledger will not discuss its second set of weights with
somebody it does not like, and that is the gate on the quest, not a separate check.

infos.x: Every gate keeps two sets. One for the book and one for the barge, and a good clerk can tell you which is which by the sound they make on the stone. A bad clerk finds out when somebody weighs him.
Eeja says the stones under the counting floor ring wrong. He has said it for two years and nobody has gone down to look, and he will not go himself because he cannot read what is chalked on them.
You want to know about weights, do you. Ask who sells the brass. There is one caster in Gideon and he has never once been asked to make a matched pair.

The wharf is owed. It has been owed since before my hatching. Every season the Ledger writes the debt forward and every season the men who carry the crates get eleven gold and the men who write it down get the rest.
It is not a debt. It is a float. The distinction matters to exactly one person in this province and she keeps the book it is written in.
I sell rope to the wharf and the wharf pays me in chits that are good at three shops. Work out for yourself who owns the three shops.
There is a chair at the table that nobody sits in and everybody argues with. That is the quiet partner. When the Ledger votes, it votes seven and one, and the one is never in the room.
I have fenced for the Ledger eleven years and I have never met the quiet partner, and I have twice been told to stop asking in words that were not friendly.
Lilmoth pays a quiet partner too. Different chair, same silence. Tesh signs for it and does not look at what she is signing, which is a skill.

A ship puts in for water. That is all it is. They fill four barrels and they lie at anchor nine days and they leave heavier than they came, and everybody on this beach knows and everybody on this beach eats.
Water is a right of the sea. No charter in the Empire denies a ship water. You will find that is the whole of the law on it, and I have found the whole of the law on it very restful.
I write the water-call in the bond book as a call for water. What is in the hold when it leaves is a question for the harbour, and the harbour has never once asked it.
My sister's egg-clutch went off that beach in a water-call. Nine days at anchor, dry-one. Nine days is not water.
An underwriter holds a gate. Not the guild's gate — a gate, one gate, and the toll off it comes to their hand before it comes to the table. It is how the Ledger makes a person expensive to lose.
You want a gate of your own? Then you had better have something the table wants more than it wants the gate, and there are only two things on that list.

The question is whether Archon is a harbour or a hole. It has been asked at the table four times in twenty years and it has been answered the same way four times, and the answer is worth about nine thousand a season.
Ask a captain here what he thinks of the question and he will ask you what you think of your teeth. The captains take the money. That is not a secret, it is an arrangement.
One cohort, under strength, and a beach twelve barges wide. If the Assize wants Archon closed it can send somebody to close it. It has not.
The first chair has been held by one person for nineteen years and she has outlived two governors and a plague. She does not eat with us. She reads what we write and then she tells us what we meant.
Nobody takes the first chair. It is taken from the person in it, and the last three people who tried are on the tally at Soulrest under names that are not theirs.

The Assize is the court and the customs and the toll book, and in this province those are one office because there was only ever budget for one. If you want a thing to be legal you come to us. If you want it to be just you go somewhere else.
Cohort holds the wall, Assize holds the pen. Ask any legionary which of the two has ever lost an argument.

You can be robbed in Gideon and get a hearing for it, which is more than they manage in Lilmoth. Whether the hearing goes your way is a different question and it has an answer, and the answer is written down in a book you are not allowed to read.

The toll book is the Assize's memory. Everything that has come up this river for forty years is in it, in the hand of whichever notary was awake. It is also, and this is not written anywhere, the only complete record of what House Dres has moved through Archon.
Two books, in fact — the fair copy that the Governor signs and the day-book the notary actually writes in, and the interesting thing about the pair is how often they differ by exactly one entry.
Blackrose leases its prisoners out. It is lawful, it is audited, and the audit is done by the office that writes the leases. I have read the roll. I would rather not have.

Labour lease. Men go out on a chit and come back on a chit and the number that go out is the number that come back, because the number that come back is written by the man who writes the number that go out.
We take the yard hands the lease sends and we do not ask where the ones from last season went. Nobody in this yard asks. It is a very quiet yard.
Sedda Vell. Struck off the roll eleven years ago for what the finding called a persistent irregularity of temper. She kept her day-books. That is the part nobody at the court will say out loud.
She drinks here. She does not talk about the court unless you buy the second one, and then she does not stop.
A notary struck off keeps nothing by right and everything in practice, because the office never asks for the books back — asking would concede the books existed.

Eleven years of leases, in a hand that got steadier the angrier she got. If it ever reaches the Elder Council it ends four careers, and three of those four have made their peace with that and the fourth has not.
I have been told twice, by people who were being kind, that the day-book does not exist. Both of them said it in the same words, which is how I know it does.

A warrant makes a killing lawful inside Imperial ground and nowhere else, and four of the people on the current roll do not live inside Imperial ground. Getting them onto it is the job. The killing is the easy part and it is not the part that goes wrong.

It clears the bounty on the name written on it. It clears nothing else — not the door you broke, not the man who got in the way, not the fourteen days after which the office takes it back and tells your target who you are.
Paper that says you may. I have seen three men wave one at a militia sergeant in Soulrest. Soulrest is not Imperial ground. Two of them are on the tally.
Hallow comes up to Gideon once a season to sign the roll and once a season the roll is already signed when he gets there. He has stopped remarking on it. That is the thing to notice.
The Prefect's return is the document that says the lease is sound. It is two pages, it is signed at Blackrose, and it has been copied out in the same Gideon hand for six seasons.
The Assize sits on it in Second Seed. Four seats. Two of them owe money to a body that is not the Empire and one of them is honest, and the honest one is not sure which way honest goes here.

If the lease falls, six hundred people walk out of Blackrose into a province with no work in it. If it stands, six hundred people do not walk anywhere. Neither of those is the good answer and the vote will pretend one of them is.
There is one seal in the province that closes a finding for good, and the Legate keeps it in a drawer he does not lock, because in nineteen years nobody has been mad enough to take it.
The Legate of the Assize answers to the Elder Council in theory and to the boat schedule in practice. Two letters a year. He has learned to write them in a way that requires no reply.
East of Helstrom on the root track there is a hollow that takes what it is given and gives back a name. That is all I will say to a stranger, and I have said more than I should.
The Deep-Kin do not have a hall, dry-one. They have a hollow, and a hollow is not a place you visit, it is a place that decides whether you arrived.
Everyone in this town knows where it is and nobody in this town will walk you there. Work out what that costs and then double it, because the price is not gold.
The track is not cut. It is agreed. Where the roots have agreed to lie flat you may walk, and where they have not you may also walk, once.
Follow the black water east until the trees stop being separate trees. Then keep the sound of the water on the same side of you the whole way, and do not put your hand on anything.
I have run cargo on the root track twice and I will not do it again for money. The second time the track was not where it was the first time.
The question is what a lukiul is. Kin who went to the coast, or coast that wears kin. Teel-Ashaan has an answer. Ee-Vashum has a different one and she buried a daughter for it.
They call us lukiul like it is a word for a thing that broke. My grandmother was born in Gideon. Where exactly was she supposed to go.
The river bands do not use the word. We say those who trade and those who do not, and we have both in the same clutch, and we manage.

The saying is that the coast cities are a wound and wounds are cut out. It is newer than people think. I heard it first nine years ago from a man who had lost four of his line at Archon, and it was not a policy then, it was a grief.
Cut the coast off and the takers stop coming. Cut the coast off and eleven thousand of our own starve behind the cut. Both of those are true and the hollow only says the first one aloud.
Bad for freight. Bad for everyone. Whoever is saying it has never had to move salt.
The sap-wells are giving back nothing. The Court at Soulrest has it as a curve. We have it as a hollow that has stopped answering and a clutch that came out wrong twice in one season.
We burn them and we count them and the count does not arrive anywhere. I have written that sentence in a ledger eleven times and each time a sexton has told me to write it differently.
Thirty years we have cut and nothing happened. Prove it was us. I will wait.

A ku-vastei is not called and does not refuse. When a thing has gone too far one arrives, hears it, and rules, and the ruling ends the blood-price whichever way it falls. You do not thank them. Thanking them suggests you had a preference.

Egg-born under the sign, given to the shadow, and sent back to us to do the one thing none of us can do without starting the next feud. I have seen two rulings. Both were correct and neither was kind.
Argonian arbiter. No standing in Imperial law whatsoever. The Cohort has stopped saying so out loud in the interior because saying so out loud was getting people hurt.
The Xul-Aneekh do not vote and do not command. A thing becomes consensus when nobody left is arguing, and there are two ways to arrive at nobody left arguing.
They will tell you it is not a government. They are right. That is what frightens the people on the coast, not the other thing.
Teel-Ashaan has spoken for the hollow for twenty-two years. A speaker stops when the hollow stops listening, and the hollow has never yet stopped listening on its own.
The last speaker before this one went quiet in a season and nobody has said how, and nobody has said how in a way that means everybody knows how.
